To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prevalence of hepatitis B markers among haemophiliac patients and their contacts was similar to that in the normal population, but that the prevalence of markers of past infection was higher in haemophilliacs than in controls.

the prevalence of anti-HBs in haemophila patients was similar to that in the general population, and the prevalence of anti- HBc was significantly higher in the patients than in the population at large.
In a group of 70 haemophiliac patients one was a carrier of hepatitis B antigen (HBs) and the remaining had antibody to hepatitis surface antigen (antiHBs) and core antigen (antiHBc).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prevalence of hepatitis B infection among haemophiliac patients and their contacts.
the detection of antibodies to hepatitis B surface (HBs) and core (HBc) antigens in haematophiliacs, and in hospital personnel who are in contact with these patients.
the epidemiological aspects of hepatitis B virus infection among patients with haemophilia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk of acquiring hepatitis B infection from the use of blood products for treatment of haemophilia is small and that the risk is not greater than that from other blood transfusions.
the haemophiliac patients and their contacts, as well as the personnel of the haemostasis laboratory, were not at risk of acquiring hepatitis B infection from the use of clotting factors.
the risk of acquiring hepatitis B infection from blood products is small and that the use of blood products in haemophila patients is safe, provided that all blood donors are screened for HBsAg.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of anti-HBs among the haemophiliac population in the United States is 97.5%.
the use of hepatitis B virus (HBV) markers is a valuable tool in the management of patients with haemophilia and their contacts.
the prevalence of hepatitis B markers in haemophilliacs and in hospital personnel is not different from that of the general population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of hepatitis B surface antibody as a surrogate marker for protection against infection with hepatitis B is a poor choice.
the risk of hepatitis B virus infection among haemophiliac patients is low.
the prevalence of HBsAg and anti-HBs in a haemophilic population reflects the quality control of the plasma used in the production of clotting-factor concentrates.
